title: Kernel tail lattice profiling notes — Dec 2026
content:
Summary:

This note captures the December 2026 investigation into persistent low‑frequency tail latency spikes we observed on production-like decoder runs. The pattern is not classic microburst or obvious preemption — instead we repeatedly see a periodic (~250ms) dip in SM occupancy that aligns with a lattice of very short kernels executing across multiple streams near the end of token generation. I’m calling this the 'kernel tail lattice' behavior.

High level hypothesis:
- Short-lived kernels (tens to hundreds of microseconds) launched in a dense interleaved pattern expose a coupling between host DMA bursts, L2 eviction noise, and SM warp starvation at the tail of generation.
- CUDA graph segmentation + async copies can amplify phased interference: when a graph replay hits a particular alignment, compounded small-launch jitter creates a lattice of idle gaps between productive kernels.

Test bed and capture details:
- HW: 8xA100 (80GB) equivalent test rig (single-GPU traces used for Nsight to reduce noise).
- Runtime: serving-runtime main @ commit b14f3c4 (batcher refactor + prefetch window 32KB).
- Model: 8B decoder (fp16 + q4 binding) sampled with deterministic prompts to align seq lengths.
- Workload: high variance tails: 80% short (<64 tokens), 20% long (200–512 tokens) sequences.
- Nsight settings: sample mode turned off; full timeline capture on 1 GPU for 45s windows, kernel-level timestamping enabled, NVTX at callsite + per‑request ids.
- Additional telemetry: host-side DMA scatter logs, kernel-launch timestamps emitted by runtime, and small tracer that logs KV cache prefetch attempts.

Canonical trace TL-20261208-01 findings:
- Timeline shows recurring ~200–300ms periods where SM active occupancy drops from ~72% to ~18% for a 5–15ms span around token finalization.
- These low‑occupancy spans align with a burst of cuMemcpyAsync from host to device (size ~12–40KB, batched) followed by ~120–300 short (<400us) kernels spread across 3 streams.
- L2 read/write stalls spike (Nsight memory counters) during those bursts; L2 miss rate increases by ~3–4x relative to baseline.
- CUDA graph replay windows (we use graph partition size 8) show that when graph boundary coincides with DMA completion, the kernel launch pacing degrades and kernels queue with slightly higher launch latency variance (sigma increases by ~30%).
- NVTX tags indicate that affected requests are disproportionately the long-tail sequences that require extra kv-prefetch iterations at end of decode.

Micro-observations and root-cause hints:
- Small DMA bursts appear to evict recently used L2 lines that short kernels expected to reuse (attention kernel fragments and rotary tables). The eviction/reload cycle costs register through L2 misses > memory latency causing thread-blocks to stall or underutilize tensor cores.
- Kernel launch pacing: freed CUDA stream slots are refilled unevenly when host threads (batcher/dispatcher) do tiny, synchronous bookkeeping work between launches. The jitter is small but when many tiny kernels are back-to-back, it sums to visible idle windows on SMs.
- Kernel sizing: our split-kernel approach generates many sub‑kernels for attention and feedforward microsteps. For long sequences we hit many of these at the tail; each individually is efficient but the graph of launches is brittle to host timing noise.

Evidence matrix (why we believe the above):
- Cross-correlation between host DMA start timestamps and SM occupancy valley shows >0.8 correlation coefficient across 25 traces.
- Replaying workloads with DMA disabled (prefetch turned off) removes the valley entirely in ~90% of captures.
- Increasing CUDA graph partition size to coalesce successive kernels into larger graphs reduces launch jitter and occupancy valleys by ~60% but increases single-kernel tail latency (tradeoff).
- Synthetic test where we coalesced tiny kernels into fused kernels (local experiment) also removes the lattice but required a non-trivial refactor to kernel fusion infra.

Immediate mitigations tried in test environment:
- Staggered host dispatch: added 50–150us intentional spacing between kernel launches — reduced occupancy valley depth but introduced a modest 1.5% p99 increase for some short requests. Not acceptable for general release.
- Increase graph partitioning: moving to larger graphs (size 32) smoothed launch variance but added ~6% increase in memory residency and made fallback logic more complex. Works as short-term patch for Dedicated nodes where memory headroom exists.
- Adjust prefetch policy: limit aggressive kv-prefetch for long requests when host is saturated. This reduced correlated DMA bursts and significantly lowered L2 miss spikes in trace.
- Stream priority: elevated inference stream priority reduced queuing time of tiny kernels when concurrent housekeeping streams were active; observable improvement in valley duration but not complete elimination.

Cost/benefit considerations:
- Kernel fusion is likely the most robust solution (fewer launches, better data locality), but it has significant engineering cost and needs careful testing across model shapes and quant modes.
- Larger CUDA graphs are lower effort but trade memory and complexity (graph replay fallback, segmentation on dynamic shapes). Preferable as a regional/hosted feature toggle for nodes with ample memory.
- Runtime-level pacing heuristics (adaptive spacing or micro-batching of tiny kernels) are lower engineering lift and can be gated behind a config flag but risk increasing p99 for small/latency‑sensitive requests.

Actionable recommendations (next steps):
1) Short term (1–2 sprints):
   - Expose a server-side config to increase default CUDA graph aggregation on Dedicated nodes and for experiments in Hosted (A/B).
   - Add detection telemetry: runtime should emit 'lattice alignment' metric when consecutive tiny-kernel launches exceed threshold N within window W and host DMA concurrent. Use this to roll out adaptive mitigations only when pattern matches.
   - Tweak kv-prefetch policy to avoid synchronized small DMAs at token finalization. Implement conservative backoff for sequences that trigger repeated L2 pressure.

2) Mid term (quarter):
   - Prototype kernel fusion for attention microsteps for one decoder block (proof-of-value). Measure throughput, memory pressure, and failure modes.
   - Investigate heuristics to dynamically choose graph partition sizes based on runtime telemetry (shape, sequence distribution, memory headroom).

3) Long term (release/roadmap):
   - Incorporate an occupancy-aware scheduler that can detect 'tail lattice' patterns and opt between fusion, graph coalescing, or pacing.
   - Harden fallback paths so that larger graphs still allow graceful fallback to segmented replay without catastrophic launch jitter.

Notes for follow-up captures:
- Capture at higher resolution (2ms buckets) around expected valley window; record nvlink counters as well — early traces focused on L2 but NVLink congestion could be contributing in multi-GPU cases.
- Collect host-side micro-profiler traces for the batcher thread — we suspect small synchronous mutexes and bookkeeping contribute to launch jitter.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How prevalent is this in customer workloads with different seq-length distributions? Our traces are biased toward produced test traffic. Need sampling from Hosted for real-world confirmation.
- Are there model architecture patterns (longer context attention + many kv-prefetches) that make this problem worse?

Appendix (quick commands used):
- Nsight capture: nsight-sys --capture-range=manual --trace=cpu,gpu --output=TL-20261208-01.nsys-rep --force
- Runtime trace collector: tools/trace_collector --nsys TL-20261208-01.nsys-rep --filter nvtx:decode_end
- Synthetic microbench: bench/small-kernel-stress --kernel-count 5000 --kernel-duration 200us --host-dma-pattern burst:12kb:repeat:50ms
